blocks.content: For rare events (accidents, tool breaks, low-rate defects) Shewhart {{term:regelkarte|control charts}} and attribute charts such as the {{term:c-chart|c chart}} are of little use: they show zeros for days and then one isolated spike that looks like an outlier. The g and t charts instead evaluate the gaps between events and take their distribution into account.

Shows the number of units or days between two consecutive events, i.e. whole numbers from 0 (geometric distribution). {{term:regelgrenze|Control limits}} per Benneyan: CL = ḡ, UCL = ḡ + 3·√(ḡ·(ḡ+1)), LCL = ḡ − 3·√(ḡ·(ḡ+1)), capped at 0. Because 3·√(ḡ·(ḡ+1)) is never smaller than ḡ, the LCL of the g chart is always 0.

Shows the time between events (continuous, exponentially distributed). The times are transformed for the analysis: y = t^(1/3.6) (Nelson 1994); values up to 0 remain as gaps. On y the limits of an individuals chart apply, ȳ ± 3·MR̄/1.128, with the LCL capped at 0. The chart plots y; the figures show center line and limits back-transformed (y^3.6) on the original scale.

A point above the UCL is an unusually long “quiet” stretch: events have become rarer, perhaps through an improvement whose cause is worth knowing. A cluster, i.e. conspicuously short gaps and thus a deterioration, shows downward. The g chart cannot report it, because its LCL is always 0 and no gap lies below it. The t chart often has an LCL above 0 on the transformed scale and can then report a cluster as a point below the LCL. The module marks only points outside the limits; it does not check run or trend rules.
The g chart needs counts between events; the t chart needs actual time durations greater than 0. Mixing them up yields nonsense limits.

The module computes from as few as two values, but the limits are not reliable then: with fewer than about 20 observations ḡ fluctuates strongly. The classic SPC rule of 25–30 points applies here too.

A cluster of events produces no point outside the limits on the g chart (LCL always 0). A run of short gaps is left to looking at the plot. If the gaps are actual time durations, the t chart can report a cluster as a point below the LCL.

Center line and limits are estimated from the whole series. If the rate changes within the series, the values after the change pull center line and limits along; the change then often produces no signal, even when it is visible in the plot.

Both charts assume the event rate is constant. With a clearly increasing rate (e.g. due to tool wear) split the data at the change and run a separate chart per segment, each segment in its own column.
